text.p: Dear Mom, Love ya... How much money have ya got?
A touch more diplomacy, and that's the sort of greeting the folks at Harris Bank in Chicago suggest we extend this Mother's Day. And they aren't wrong.

More than half of the women who responded to a recent financial survey said they never discuss finances with their parents, and most of them said they had little understanding of what their parents would want done with their money or health care should they become unable to make their own decisions.

Couple that lack of communication with the mistakes many people make in creating estate plans (or not creating them at all) and it seems like it's time to talk about money. Or, as Harris Bank says, this Mother's Day, "remember the gift of information."

As a mother and a daughter, I instead submit that on Mother's Day you remember the gift of the card, the flowers, the perfume or whatever, and save the financial chat just a little bit longer. You can talk about money on Monday.
Then, talk about money. If talking makes everybody nervous, writing about money is probably even more helpful.

A few books to get you started include "The Beneficiary Book" by Martin Kuritz, John Sampson and David Sanchez ($29.95, Viking, 1996) and "Everything Your Heirs Need to Know ($19.95, Dearborn Financial Publishing, 1995). Both books offer guided fill-in-the-blanks formats to family financial and health history.

Some of the issues that your parents or your children might be reluctant to discuss, but which they probably worry about concern the personal side of these plans: Who will make health care decisions, who will raise minor children, to what priorities will money flow.
Some areas to discuss or record, according to Harris Vice President Judy Phillips, include the following:

-- Where's the will? It should exist, of course, and be updated regularly as the family changes. Keep one copy in a safe place such as a safe deposit box, a second with the intended executor and a third with the attorney who wrote it.

-- What are the medical wishes? A durable health care power of attorney transfers the power to make medical decisions, such as whether or not to undergo risky surgical procedures or outlining your preferred approach to life-prolonging measures.

-- What about non-estate assets? Retirement accounts, insurance policy proceeds and trusts move to their beneficiaries outside of the will-driven estate. So make sure the beneficiaries designated are the ones that were intended.
-- Where's the money? Everyone should maintain a central list of their bank and investment accounts.
-- Who else knows about this? Are their attorneys, brokers, accountants or other financial professionals who handle your finances? Who are they? Another list, please.

These are important bits of information that should be kept up to date but don't need to be discussed endlessly. So open the topic, take the necessary notes and put it away. If you start now you can be done before Father's Day!
